scan.summary: This is the company's own written food safety plan for the Salem plant, built under the FDA preventive controls rule for human food (21 CFR Part 117, Subpart C), and the same plan the Oregon Department of Agriculture will ask to see when it inspects the licensed processing establishment. It is an internal program document, not an agency approval, so it is judged against the rule: the process, allergen and sanitation controls for cooking, cooling, metal detection and labelling are written out in usable detail, but several parts the rule requires as part of the plan are absent or thin. The plan is unsigned, carries an effective date of 12 May 2025 and no revision history, and the three-year reanalysis the rule requires falls due 12 May 2028 at the latest.
scan.freshness_note: Effective 12 May 2025 — about sixteen months old at 27 September 2026. That is not stale for a food safety plan, but there is no revision history, no signature and no record of any reanalysis since it took effect, so ask whether a later revision exists before relying on this copy.

gaps.title: Refrigerated storage hazard has no control, limit or monitoring
gaps.description: The hazard analysis says refrigerated storage of a 45-day-shelf-life RTE product needs a preventive control for Listeria growth, but section 4 has no control or critical limit for storage temperature and section 5 assigns nobody to monitor it.
gaps.fix: Add a process preventive control for refrigerated storage and shipping — critical limit at or below 41°F, continuous or at least twice-daily recorded checks of each cooler, named monitor, and a corrective action for excursions. The plan already states the 41°F holding temperature, so the text can be drafted from what is here.
gaps.locator: Section 3 (page 3, "Refrigerated storage" row) and section 4 (page 4) / section 5 (page 5)
gaps.quote: Refrigerated storage Growth of Listeria monocytogenes Biological Yes Refrigerated RTE product with a 45-day shelf life

gaps.title: Environmental monitoring and product testing have no written procedure
gaps.description: The plan names weekly Listeria swabs at 10 sites and monthly finished product testing, but gives no written procedure: no sampling plan or site map, no laboratory method, no test result interpretation, no corrective action procedure tied to the testing, no identification of the laboratory.
gaps.fix: Write out the environmental monitoring and finished product testing procedures as required — site selection and rotation, zones, timing relative to production, sample collection method, analytical method, laboratory, and the actions on a presumptive positive — and attach them to the plan.
gaps.quote: Finished product is tested for Listeria monocytogenes monthly by an accredited laboratory. Environmental monitoring results are trended quarterly.

gaps.title: No reanalysis provision
gaps.description: Nothing in the plan says it will be reanalysed at least every three years, or on a significant change, new hazard information, an unanticipated food safety problem, or a finding that a control is ineffective, and nothing says the PCQI performs or oversees that reanalysis.
gaps.fix: Add a reanalysis section stating the three-year cycle, the four trigger events, that the PCQI performs or oversees it, and that the plan is revised or the no-change conclusion documented. Confirmed against the current text of the rule: reanalysis of the plan as a whole is required at least once every 3 years.

gaps.title: No written recall plan
gaps.description: The plan identifies hazards requiring preventive controls, which triggers the requirement for a written recall plan, and there is none — no notification steps, no procedure to retrieve or dispose of recalled product, no effectiveness checks, no public notice decision.
gaps.fix: Write the recall plan as a numbered section of this food safety plan: who directs a recall, how consignees in Oregon, Washington and Idaho are notified, how FDA and ODA are notified, how product is retrieved and disposed of, how effectiveness is checked, and when public notification is used. The distribution and coding information already in the plan supports a draft.

gaps.title: Supply-chain program is too thin for Subpart G
gaps.description: Section 8 is three lines. It does not say which hazards, if any, are controlled by a supplier; it does not state supplier approval criteria, the supplier verification activity chosen for each hazard and why, who conducts and documents the verification, or how receiving is controlled for unapproved suppliers.
gaps.fix: Either state in the hazard analysis that no hazard requiring a preventive control is controlled before receipt (the bean foreign-material hazard is currently said to be controlled in part by supplier screening, which points the other way), or build the Subpart G program out: written procedures for receiving, approval of suppliers, the verification activity per supplier and hazard, and records of each. Which of 117.405–117.435 bind this plant turns on that determination, which I cannot settle from the document.
gaps.quote: Tahini and dry beans are received only from approved suppliers who provide a current third-party audit certificate and a certificate of analysis for each lot.

gaps.title: Training records not mentioned
gaps.description: Section 10 describes training but says nothing about documenting it. The rule requires records of the required training — who was trained, in what, by whom, on what date.
gaps.fix: Add a line to section 10 that training is documented on a training record showing date, trainee, subject and trainer, retained with the plan's records, and that the PCQI's qualification certificate is on file.
gaps.quote: All production employees receive food hygiene training at hire and annually. The PCQI holds a current FSPCA certificate.

gaps.title: Corrective actions do not cover unanticipated problems or corrections
gaps.description: Section 6 lists a response for each named deviation but has no general procedure for a problem nobody anticipated, and it does not address corrections — minor, timely fixes to a sanitation or allergen issue made before product is affected. It also does not state the four steps every corrective action must take (identify and correct, reduce recurrence, evaluate affected food, prevent adulterated food entering commerce).
gaps.fix: Add a general corrective action procedure covering unanticipated food safety problems, including the four required steps and the requirement to reanalyse the plan where appropriate, plus a short paragraph on corrections and how they are recorded.
gaps.quote: All corrective actions are recorded on the corrective action log and reviewed by the PCQI within seven days.

gaps.title: Plan is not signed and dated
gaps.description: The cover page names a preparer and says "Approved by: Plant Manager" but carries no signature and no signature date. The rule requires the owner, operator or agent in charge to sign and date the plan on completion and on any modification.
gaps.fix: Have the owner, operator or agent in charge sign and date the cover page, and re-sign on each revision. Keep a revision table showing version, date and what changed.

gaps.title: No validation of the process preventive controls
gaps.description: There is no validation of the cook and the cooling controls — no scientific or technical basis for 212°F for 60 minutes or for the 135°F–70°F–41°F cooling schedule, and no statement that the PCQI performed or oversaw validation.
gaps.fix: Attach the validation: the scientific basis for each process control (cooling schedule references a recognised cooling standard; the cook lethality basis), dated and signed by the PCQI. Validation must be performed or overseen by the PCQI before implementation, or within 90 days of first production with written justification for longer.
gaps.quote: Cook beans in the kettle to an internal temperature of at least 212°F for at least 60 minutes

gaps.title: Hazard analysis omits chemical hazards and economically motivated adulteration
gaps.description: The table covers biological, physical and allergen hazards only. There is no evaluation of chemical hazards — pesticide or mycotoxin residues in beans, sanitizer residue on food-contact surfaces, heavy metals or radiological hazards — and no consideration of hazards intentionally introduced for economic gain, which matters for olive oil, tahini and spices.
gaps.fix: Add rows for chemical hazards at each step where they are reasonably foreseeable, and a line evaluating economically motivated adulteration for the purchased ingredients most exposed to it (olive oil, spices, tahini), with the conclusion and its justification.
gaps.quote: Step Hazard Type Requires a preventive control? Justification

gaps.title: Record content requirements not stated
gaps.description: Section 9 covers where records are kept and for how long, but not what every record must show: the plant name and location, the actual observed values, the date and time of the activity, and the signature or initials of the person doing the work and of the reviewer, with the date of review.
gaps.fix: Add a short paragraph to section 9 stating the required content of every record and that records are created at the time the activity is performed, accurate, indelible and legible.
gaps.quote: All records named in this plan are kept at the Salem plant for at least two years from the date of the record

gaps.title: Retention rule does not cover records supporting the food safety plan
gaps.description: Section 9 gives one blanket rule — two years from the date of the record. Records that support the plan itself, such as validation studies, scientific justifications and the basis for hazard decisions, are held to a different clock: at least two years after their use is discontinued.
gaps.fix: Split the retention statement into the two cases: records of monitoring, corrective actions, verification and training retained at least two years after they are made; records supporting the plan retained at least two years after their use is discontinued. I am confident of the section number here but suggest confirming the exact wording of 117.315 before adopting it verbatim.
gaps.quote: All records named in this plan are kept at the Salem plant for at least two years from the date of the record and are available to FDA and the Oregon Department of Agriculture on request.

gaps.title: Allergen changeover washdown is a control with no assigned monitoring
gaps.description: The allergen preventive control requires a full washdown after the hummus run with ATP verification before the next non-sesame product. Section 5 only assigns an ATP swab before each start-up; nobody is named to monitor the mid-run allergen changeover, and no frequency or record is stated for it.
gaps.fix: Name the monitor, the swab sites, the acceptance limit and the log for the allergen changeover washdown in section 5, so the allergen control has monitoring of its own as the rule requires. The control text in section 4 gives enough to draft from.
gaps.citation: 21 CFR 117.140(a) and 117.145 (monitoring of the allergen preventive control)
gaps.quote: washdown verified by ATP swab before the next non-sesame product

scan.confidence_notes: The document read cleanly — all seven pages, all ten sections, all four tables — so every quote above is text actually in the file. I am confident about the identification (a Part 117 Subpart C food safety plan, company-authored, Salem site, federal rule plus Oregon ODA oversight) and about the eleven gaps that match the earlier reading; each is a plain absence I can point at. I am confident of the reanalysis rule (three years, checked against the current regulation text) and of the validation timing rule. Two things I am less sure of: whether any hazard here is in fact controlled by a supplier, which decides how much of Subpart G binds this plant — the bean foreign-material row says supplier screening is part of the control, which points towards Subpart G applying, but the plan never says so outright; and the exact wording of the record retention rule, where I am sure of the section but suggest checking the text before copying it. The 12 May 2028 reanalysis date is inferred from the effective date, not printed in the document. I have not verified whether a later signed revision of this plan exists.

WILLAMETTE VALLEY FOODS, INC.
FOOD SAFETY PLAN
Ready-to-eat hummus and bean dips
Salem Plant, 1850 Fairgrounds Road NE, Salem, Oregon 97301
Effective date: May 12, 2025
Prepared by: Dana Whitfield, Quality Manager, Preventive Controls Qualified Individual
(PCQI certificate, FSPCA course, March 2024)
Approved by: Plant Manager
1. Facility and product description
Willamette Valley Foods produces refrigerated ready-to-eat hummus and bean dips in 8-ounce and 16-
ounce sealed plastic tubs for retail sale in Oregon, Washington and Idaho. The Salem plant operates one
shift, five days a week, with 28 production employees. Products are made from cooked chickpeas or black
beans, tahini, lemon juice, garlic, olive oil, salt and spices, blended, filled, sealed, coded and held
refrigerated at or below 41°F. Shelf life is 45 days refrigerated. Products are labeled with the allergen
statement "Contains: sesame" for all hummus items.
2. Process flow
Receiving of dry beans, tahini and other ingredients → dry storage or refrigerated storage → soaking and
cooking of beans (kettle, 212°F, 60 minutes minimum) → cooling in the blast chiller → blending with
other ingredients → filling and sealing → date coding → metal detection → refrigerated storage →
shipping.

5. Monitoring
The kettle operator records the internal temperature and the time at the start and end of each cook batch
on the cook log. The blast chiller operator records the temperature at 2 hours and at 6 hours on the cooling
log. The sanitation lead records the ATP swab result before each start-up. The line lead runs the three
metal test pieces through the detector at start-up, every two hours, and at the end of the run, and records
the result. The quality technician reviews every label lot against the formulation sheet at receipt and signs
the label log.
6. Corrective actions
If a cook batch does not reach 212°F for 60 minutes, the batch is re-cooked to the critical limit or
discarded, and the cause is recorded. If cooling exceeds the time limits, the batch is discarded. If an ATP
swab fails, the surface is re-cleaned and re-swabbed before production starts. If a Listeria spp. swab is
positive, the site is cleaned and re-swabbed, adjacent sites are added, and product made on that line since
the last negative swab is held pending investigation. If the metal detector fails a test piece, all product
since the last passing test is re-run through the detector. If a label does not match the formulation, the lot
is quarantined and not used. All corrective actions are recorded on the corrective action log and reviewed
by the PCQI within seven days.
7. Verification
The PCQI reviews the cook, cooling, sanitation, allergen and metal detection records within seven
working days of their creation. Probe thermometers are calibrated in ice water and boiling water weekly,
and the metal detector is serviced by the manufacturer annually. Finished product is tested for Listeria
monocytogenes monthly by an accredited laboratory. Environmental monitoring results are trended
quarterly.
8. Supply-chain program
Tahini and dry beans are received only from approved suppliers who provide a current third-party audit
certificate and a certificate of analysis for each lot. The approved supplier list is maintained by the quality
manager.
9. Records
All records named in this plan are kept at the Salem plant for at least two years from the date of the record
and are available to FDA and the Oregon Department of Agriculture on request. Records are reviewed and
signed by the PCQI as described in section 7.
10. Training
All production employees receive food hygiene training at hire and annually. The PCQI holds a current
FSPCA certificate. Sanitation and line leads are trained on the monitoring procedures in this plan.
